case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
case.limits: The court read the statute's word individual and expressly left open how much AI assistance a human inventor may use. The unsettled question is inventorship quality, not machine inventorship, which is closed.
case.holding: An inventor under the Patent Act must be a natural person, so a patent application naming an AI system as the sole inventor is properly refused without reaching whether the system actually conceived anything.

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The controlling answer to AI-invented subject matter: whatever a system devises, the application must name a human inventor. Companies cite it when structuring filings around human contributors; challengers cite it to attack patents where the human contribution looks nominal.

reading.body:
The only question *Thaler v. Vidal* settled is whether an AI system can be named as a sole inventor on a United States patent application: it cannot, because the Patent Act's word "individual" requires a natural person.

The Federal Circuit reached that holding without deciding whether the AI system in question actually conceived anything. That distinction is consequential. A company can satisfy *Thaler* by placing a human name on a filing, but the court expressly left open how much AI assistance that human may have used and still qualify as an inventor. The line between a genuine human conception and a nominal one remains undrawn, which is precisely why both applicants and challengers cite the case, in opposite directions, when the human contribution looks thin.

For AI development, the practical pressure is on documentation: teams that use AI heavily in the invention process now bear the burden of establishing what the human contributors actually did, before filing and in anticipation of challenge. The data covers the inventorship question only. It does not address downstream questions about patent validity, claim scope, or how courts will evaluate the quality of human contribution when that question is eventually litigated.
